definition: A system architecture where a cheap, fast model attempts a task first, escalating to a more powerful (and expensive) model only when needed, such as when confidence is low.
details: Model cascades aim to reduce average inference cost by reserving expensive model calls for genuinely difficult cases, while still handling most requests with a lightweight first-pass model.

explainer.lead: A model cascade lets a small, inexpensive model handle the easy work and calls in a stronger model only for difficult cases. This can keep most responses fast and cheap without giving up the extra capability needed for the hard ones.

tiers.eli5: Imagine doing homework with a friend: you answer the easy questions yourself and ask a teacher only when you are stuck. A model cascade works the same way, with a quick, cheap model going first and a stronger model helping when needed. The aim is to save time and money while still solving the hard problems.
tiers.practitioner: A common setup runs a lightweight model first, estimates its confidence, and escalates requests below a chosen threshold to a more capable model. The threshold needs tuning against both inference cost and answer quality, because confidence scores can be poorly calibrated. It is also important to measure end-to-end latency and errors introduced by the routing decision, not just savings on expensive model calls.
tiers.paperLevel: Let m_c be a cheap model with cost c_c and m_e an expensive model with cost c_e, where c_c < c_e. A router uses m_c(x) when its confidence is at least a threshold t and m_e(x) otherwise, giving expected cost c_c + P(escalation) * c_e when every request uses the first model. Savings depend on the escalation rate, while overall quality is limited by how reliably confidence or another routing signal identifies difficult inputs.

explainer.example: A support assistant receives “What are your opening hours?” and the lightweight model answers confidently, so no expensive call is made. For a vague request involving several account problems, its confidence is low, so the request is escalated to the stronger model.

usedIn.name: Customer support
usedIn.detail: Routine questions can stay with a lightweight model, while unclear or complex requests are escalated.

usedIn.name: Document processing
usedIn.detail: Straightforward documents can use a fast first pass, with difficult cases sent to a stronger model.

usedIn.name: Coding assistants
usedIn.detail: Simple programming requests can be handled cheaply, reserving expensive calls for harder tasks.

explainer.intuition: Not every request needs the most powerful model. A cascade spends extra compute only where the first model appears unable to do the job well.
howItWorks: Send the incoming request to a cheap, fast model.
Evaluate its answer or a confidence signal from the first pass.
Return the answer directly when the request appears to be handled well.
Escalate low-confidence or otherwise difficult cases to a stronger, more expensive model.
Use the stronger model's answer for those escalated requests.
explainer.whyItMatters: Cascades can reduce average inference cost because expensive models process only a fraction of requests. They offer a practical way to balance response quality, speed, and spending.
misconceptions: A cascade is not the same as simply making one model smaller; it uses multiple models and a routing decision.
Low confidence does not guarantee a wrong answer, and high confidence does not guarantee a correct one.
Escalating every difficult-looking request does not remove the first-pass cost, so savings depend on how often escalation happens.

nodes.label: Stronger model
